title: Trump Uses Defense Production Act to Lock In Critical Minerals, Samsung Warns Chip Shortage Through 2028, OWAReaper Reveals New Russian Cyber Threat
subhead: The US moves to block e-waste exports and retain rare earths domestically, Samsung signals AI memory scarcity will persist for years, and a sophisticated Russian implant targeting Exchange servers exposes the limits of standard incident response.

sections.heading: Trump Invokes Defense Production Act to Block Critical Mineral Exports
sections.body:
President Trump signed a presidential determination on Thursday delegating authority under the Defense Production Act to the Commerce Department to restrict exports of recoverable critical minerals and materials — effectively blocking the overseas shipment of electronic waste containing rare earths, tungsten, lithium, and other strategic elements.

The order targets what officials call a significant blind spot: the US exports nearly 33,000 metric tons per month of e-waste — old batteries, permanent magnets, and shredded 'black mass' from battery recycling — much of it ultimately processed in China. By keeping those materials in-country, the administration aims to feed a domestic recycling industry that has struggled to compete with global buyers paying above-market rates for scrap.

The move is the latest in a string of actions this year. In January, Trump issued a proclamation based on a Commerce Department finding that processed critical mineral imports threaten national security. On July 20, he signed an order making it harder for defense contractors to obtain waivers allowing purchases of critical minerals from prohibited foreign suppliers. The January 2027 deadline for defense contractors to stop buying Chinese minerals entirely adds urgency.

The stakes are particularly acute for tungsten: the US has not commercially mined it since 2015, and world supply remains dominated by Chinese production. The recycler Amermin wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in March that tungsten exports pose 'an unacceptable risk to American industrial and military readiness.' Meanwhile, North American recyclers Li-Cycle and Ascend Elements have both filed for bankruptcy in the past 18 months, underscoring the fragility of the domestic processing base the order is meant to strengthen.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first use of the DPA specifically to retain minerals already inside the US rather than to stimulate new production. It acknowledges that building new mines takes years, but recapturing scrap can scale faster — if the recycling capacity exists. Whether it works depends on whether domestic processors can absorb the material currently flowing overseas.

sections.heading: Samsung Reports Record Profit, Warns AI Memory Shortage Will Last Through 2028
sections.body:
Samsung Electronics reported a more than 250-fold jump in chip profit for Q2 2026, with operating profit reaching KRW 89.5 trillion (roughly $62 billion) — the highest quarterly figure in the company's history. The surge was driven by explosive demand for AI memory, with Samsung's memory division hitting all-time highs in revenue.

But the more consequential signal came in Samsung's forward guidance: the company forecast that AI memory chip shortages will worsen through 2027 and extend into 2028, and announced it has signed long-term supply agreements with major customers to lock in capacity. Rival SK Hynix also posted a 557% profit surge for Q2, yet saw its stock sell off on revenue misses — a sign that even record earnings aren't satisfying markets expecting infinite demand.

The dual message is clear: the AI infrastructure buildout is creating a more durable memory shortage than previous cycles, and the major Korean suppliers are positioning themselves for years of pricing power. Samsung's shares surged 8% on the shortage forecast, while memory-related stocks across Micron, SanDisk, AMD, and Intel rallied up to 23%.
sections.whyItMatters: Samsung's 2028 shortage warning is the most explicit timeline yet from a major producer. It signals that AI memory supply constraints are not a temporary bottleneck but a multi-year gap between demand and fab capacity — with implications for everything from GPU availability to data center construction costs.

sections.heading: OWAReaper: Russian State Hackers Deploy Exchange Implant That Survives Re-Imaging
sections.body:
Cybersecurity firm Proofpoint disclosed on July 29 a previously unknown browser-based implant called OWAReaper, deployed by Russian state-linked hacking group Laundry Bear (also tracked as TA488 and Void Blizzard by Microsoft) against US and European government agencies and critical-sector organizations.

The implant exploits CVE-2026-42897, a cross-site scripting flaw in Outlook Web Access that Microsoft disclosed on May 14 and confirmed was already under active exploitation. Opening a maliciously crafted email in OWA is sufficient to trigger the payload — no clicks, no attachments, no links needed. Proofpoint calls this a 'half-click' exploit.

What makes OWAReaper unusual is its persistence architecture. Layer one encrypts itself in OWA's localStorage, piggybacking on OWA's own sync routine to re-execute every time a user opens a browser tab. Layer two injects hidden iframes into the browser's IndexedDB offline cache, meaning the implant can repopulate even on a freshly re-imaged machine that reconnects to the same Exchange server. Changing passwords does not remove it. Wiping and re-imaging the machine does not remove it. Only a deliberate audit and correction of Exchange folder permissions clears it.

The campaign began July 22 — one day before a joint advisory from the NSA, CISA, and allied agencies warned that the same group was simultaneously attacking Zimbra webmail servers. The phishing emails carried deliberately mundane subject lines like 'Semiconductor Supply Chain Indicators: Capacity, Packaging, and Pricing' — designed to blend in with ordinary business correspondence.
sections.whyItMatters: OWAReaper exposes a gap in standard incident response: organizations that think they've cleaned up by resetting passwords and re-imaging machines are still compromised. The implant's reliance on Exchange-side persistence rather than endpoint-side storage means the threat model for webmail has fundamentally shifted.

sections.heading: Minnesota Water Attacks Now Formally Linked to Iran, CISA Issues Nationwide Alert
sections.body:
A leaked memo from the Water Information Sharing and Analysis Center (WaterISAC), obtained by WIRED, formally ties the coordinated cyberattacks on more than 30 Minnesota water and wastewater systems to Iran-affiliated hackers — specifically to the same campaign CISA first described in April as carried out by 'Iran-affiliated' actors.

Cybersecurity firm Tenable reported that the operational pattern is consistent with CyberAv3ngers, an IRGC-linked group with a long track record of targeting small water utilities. The attacks on July 26-27 disabled automated control systems across multiple communities. In Braham (population 1,700), the attack shut down the well and water treatment plant for several hours, leaving the city reliant on its water tower reserves. In Plymouth (population 80,000), infrastructure communications were disrupted but operations continued manually. Multiple communities issued boil-water notices.

CISA issued a new advisory on July 30 warning that 'these threat actors are targeting water entities of all sizes' and urging operators to disconnect PLCs from the internet, enable strong passwords, and allowlist only trusted devices. The advisory specifically flagged that attackers modified PLC passwords to lock out operators and changed IP addresses to disconnect controllers — and noted the targeting extends to PLCs from Rockwell, Schneider Electric, and Siemens.

Former FBI cyber division deputy assistant director Cynthia Kaiser said the attacks should be treated as Iranian until proven otherwise: 'When it walks like a duck and talks like a duck, it's really important to call it out.'
sections.whyItMatters: This is the widest and most disruptive state-sponsored cyberattack on US civilian infrastructure since the Iran conflict began — and one of the most significant on US water systems ever documented. CISA's advisory makes clear this isn't a one-off: the same tradecraft and tooling can be applied to water systems across the country.

sections.heading: China Threatens Retaliation Over US Robot Ban as AI Hegemonism Dispute Deepens
sections.body:
China's commerce ministry said it will 'resolutely retaliate' if the US proceeds with the FCC's ban on foreign-made advanced robots and power inverters, which took effect this week citing national security risks. The ban targets humanoid robots and grid-scale power inverters, primarily those made in China, though it has also created confusion about whether consumer robot vacuums are affected (the FCC says they are not).

The robot ban follows a broader pattern of escalation. On July 22, White House science advisor Michael Kratsios posted that the US had 'information that Moonshot AI distilled Anthropic's Fable for the development of its K3 model,' and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent followed with sanctions threats. China's commerce ministry accused the US of 'AI hegemonism' and warned of countermeasures.

The timing is awkward for both sides. Moonshot's Kimi K3 — a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model released July 16 and published in full on July 27 — is the most powerful Chinese AI model yet made freely available. It reportedly rivals top US models on many benchmarks. But researchers noted that Fable 5 launched July 1, making a 15-day distillation timeline implausible for a model of K3's size — suggesting the accusation may be more political than technical.

Meanwhile, the NYT reported that China's own leadership is increasingly ambivalent: Xi Jinping said the government needs to 'constantly refine measures to forestall loss of control' even as it promotes openness, reflecting concerns that powerful open models could circumvent censorship and be used by adversaries against China itself.
sections.whyItMatters: The AI hegemonism dispute is shifting from a US-China narrative into a more complicated dynamic where both governments are simultaneously trying to promote and control the same technology. China's open-weight strategy is winning global adoption, but Beijing's own censorship concerns undermine the 'openness' pitch.

sections.heading: NROL-95 Launch Highlights NRO's Dual-Track Space Architecture
sections.body:
SpaceX launched the classified NROL-95 mission from Cape Canaveral at 3:10 AM ET on July 30, carrying what analysts believe is a next-generation Naval Ocean Surveillance System (NOSS) satellite — a signals intelligence platform designed to track ships by intercepting their radar and radio emissions without emitting anything itself.

The launch is notable because it reveals a deliberate dual-track architecture at the NRO. The three prior NRO missions of 2026 (NROL-105, NROL-172, NROL-179) all launched from Vandenberg carrying satellites for the proliferated Starshield constellation — a broadband ISR network built from hardened Starlink derivatives. NROL-95 is different in almost every dimension: East Coast launch, different orbital regime, and a fundamentally different mission (passive signals collection rather than active imaging and relay).

SpaceX is also the primary spacecraft vendor for both tracks. In May, it secured a $4.16 billion contract for SB-AMTI satellites (space-based air moving target indication) and a $2.29 billion contract for the Space Data Network. This week's $1.6 billion launch contract covers 18 Falcon 9 flights through 2027 from Vandenberg, pushing the total NSSL Phase 3 Lane 1 ceiling to $17 billion.

The message is clear: the NRO is building two complementary but architecturally distinct systems simultaneously, and SpaceX is building and launching both of them.
sections.whyItMatters: NROL-95 demonstrates that the proliferated constellation model and traditional specialized intelligence satellites are not substitutes but complements. SpaceX's dominant position as both launch provider and prime contractor for both architectures gives it an unprecedented role in US intelligence infrastructure.

bottomLine: Three developments stand out today. First, the Trump administration's use of the Defense Production Act to retain critical minerals in e-waste is a pragmatic acknowledgment that new mines take years but scrap reclamation can scale faster — though domestic recycling capacity remains fragile. Second, Samsung's warning that AI memory shortages will persist through 2028 reshapes the timeline for the global AI buildout, giving Korean suppliers years of pricing leverage and pressuring everyone else to secure long-term deals. Third, the convergence of state-sponsored cyber threats — OWAReaper from Russia and Iran-linked attacks on US water systems — shows that critical infrastructure targeting has become standard operating procedure for multiple adversaries simultaneously, and that conventional incident response practices are inadequate against the persistence mechanisms now being deployed.
